questions.q: What does await fetch(url) resolve to?
options: The parsed JSON data directly
A Response object, with the body read separately
A plain string of the URL
undefined until response.json() is called
questions.explain: fetch() resolves to a Response object once status/headers arrive; the body must be read and parsed as a separate step, e.g. with response.json().

questions.q: Why does fetching and parsing JSON typically require two await calls?
options: It's a stylistic choice with no real reason
fetch() resolving (headers/status) and response.json() resolving (parsed body) are two separate asynchronous steps
JavaScript requires exactly two awaits per function
The first await is only for error checking
questions.explain: The response arriving and the body being fully read and parsed are genuinely separate asynchronous operations, each with its own promise.

questions.q: If a server returns a 404 Not Found, what does fetch() do?
options: It rejects the promise automatically
It resolves the promise normally — response.ok will be false, but no rejection occurs
It throws a SyntaxError
It retries the request automatically
questions.explain: fetch() only rejects on network-level failures; an HTTP error status like 404 or 500 still resolves successfully, so checking response.ok is the caller's job.

questions.q: In the getEthPrice() example, what does the function return if the fetch or the status check fails?
options: It throws an uncaught exception
It returns null, after logging the error inside a catch block
It returns undefined with no logging
It retries the request indefinitely
questions.explain: The try/catch wraps both the network call and the manually-thrown status error, logging the failure and returning null instead of letting anything escape uncaught.

questions.q: What is the benefit of wrapping fetch, response.ok checking, and JSON parsing inside one function like getEthPrice?
options: It makes the API respond faster
Calling code doesn't need to know about fetch, Response objects, or rejections — it just awaits a value or checks for null
It removes the need for async/await entirely
It bypasses CORS restrictions
questions.explain: Encapsulating the complexity once means every caller gets a simple, predictable interface instead of repeating fetch/parsing/error-handling logic everywhere.
